title: Parity Flips at Every Step
statement:
You get an integer array nums. Return true if every pair of neighbours has different parity: one even and one odd. In other words, walking through the array, the parity must flip at every step.

An array with one element has no neighbours and counts as true.

examples.why: even, odd, even, odd, even: it flips every time.
5 and 9 are both odd. Having both parities in the array is not enough; every neighbouring pair must differ.
A single element has no neighbouring pair to break the rule.

hints: You only ever need to look at two neighbours at a time.
x % 2 gives the parity. Compare it for each i and i + 1.
Return false on the first pair with equal parity; return true if the loop finishes.

explain.intuition:
The rule is local: it only talks about neighbours. So one pass that checks each pair (nums[i], nums[i + 1]) is enough. Two numbers have the same parity exactly when nums[i] % 2 === nums[i + 1] % 2, or equivalently when their sum is even.

The trap is reading the rule globally, such as "the array contains both evens and odds" or "half are even". Those miss a pair of odds sitting next to each other.
pitfalls: Starting the loop at 0 and reading nums[-1] (undefined in JavaScript, the last element in Python).
Checking the array as a whole (both parities present, or counts balanced) instead of every neighbouring pair.
Stopping one pair early with i < n − 1 on a loop that compares i with i − 1, which skips the last pair.

solutions.title: Check every neighbouring pair
solutions.idea: Equal parity in any adjacent pair breaks the rule.

solutions.title: Match against the expected parity
solutions.idea: Once the first element fixes the starting parity, position i must have parity (first + i) % 2.

followups: Answer many queries "does the parity flip at every step inside nums[from..to]?". What do you precompute?
Return the length of the longest stretch where the parity flips at every step.
